label: Invariant Theory
notes: This chapter runs from printed pages 351 through 392 and studies polynomials unchanged by a finite group of linear substitutions. The invariants form a ring, and the central questions are finding generators, the relations among them, and how the algorithms of earlier chapters compute both effectively.

label: Group Actions on Polynomials
notes: A finite matrix group acts on the polynomial ring by linear changes of variable. A polynomial is invariant when every group element leaves it fixed. The symmetric group permuting variables is the guiding example, and its invariants are the classical symmetric polynomials studied since antiquity.

label: Symmetric Polynomials
notes: The fundamental theorem of symmetric polynomials states every symmetric polynomial is a unique polynomial in the elementary symmetric functions. A division-based algorithm rewrites any symmetric polynomial in terms of these generators, the prototype for the general invariant theory that follows.

label: The Reynolds Operator
notes: Averaging a polynomial over the group, the Reynolds operator, projects onto the invariants and produces invariant polynomials from arbitrary ones. Applied to all monomials up to the group order, it generates the full invariant ring, made finite by Noether's degree bound.

label: Generators of Invariants
notes: Noether's theorem guarantees the invariant ring of a finite group is generated by finitely many invariants of degree at most the group order. The Reynolds operator together with this bound yields an explicit finite generating set, computable directly with linear algebra and Grobner bases.

label: Relations Among Invariants
notes: The generators usually satisfy polynomial relations, called syzygies, computed by elimination from the defining equations of the generating map. The invariant ring is then presented as a quotient by these relations, completing the algorithmic picture. Next: projective algebraic geometry.
